summary: Instagram is doing most of the work: almost every Hindi video gets 1,000+ views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly get under 60 views. The best videos are the ones with a surprising claim about a robot or sensor (like 'it can't see, it only hears') and a strong visual demo; they get more likes, saves and shares. Dry 'how does X work?' videos about everyday places (lifts, taps, malls, smoke alarms) and the newest posts are getting much less attention.
winningPattern: Short Hindi videos about robots or sensors that do something surprising or 'dumb but clever' (gyro-less robot falling, clap switch hearing noise, line follower with no brain, mic as reverse speaker). Titles open with a bold, counter-intuitive claim in Hinglish ('X ko Y nahi pata, sirf Z karta hai') plus one emoji and #shorts, and the Instagram Reel is the main engine. Robot and sound-based Arduino-module topics beat everyday-building topics, and series-style follow-ups on a proven topic (clap switch) hold up on both platforms.
doMore: Lead with a bold myth-busting claim about robots and Arduino modules, e.g. 'X doesn't do what you think'.
Make follow-ups to the top hits: gyro, clap switch, PIR, line follower, mic/speaker.
Show a visible failure or demo in the first second (robot falling, switch triggering) before explaining.
End with a share or save prompt like 'Save this for your next project' since saves and shares signal quality.
Check why the IR robot video got 10 IG shares but few YouTube views, and test a different YouTube title and thumbnail for the same topic.
stopDoing: Stop making 'Kaise kaam karta hai?' videos about everyday places (lift, mall door, washroom tap, street light); they get the lowest views.
Stop posting near-duplicate topics (three smoke, two tap, two IR videos) within days of each other.
Stop posting English-only or mixed-language titles that break the Hindi pattern, and don't expect YouTube to carry the channel until its titles and hooks are tested.
